sources.title: Nebraska State Historical Society, Marker Monday: Boot Hill
sources.supports: Ogallala cowtown burials in the 1870s and 1880s used wooden headboards.
sources.limits: Historical interpretation, not a measured cemetery plan. Download returned 403; text read through browser.

sources.title: Keith County Visitors Committee, Boot Hill Walking Tour, printed 2016, Karyn Stansberry introduction
sources.supports: Introduction describes a prairie promontory, early plank or rough-cross markers, and later restoration/tree planting. Both pages visually read.
sources.limits: Modern guide and reconstructed marker photographs. No original dimensions, precise marker shapes, paint colours or six-grave plan established. Gateway and statues are later additions.

sources.title: USDA NRCS Official Series Description: Keith, 2006
sources.supports: Western Nebraska upland soil analogue: brown loess-derived topsoil; native range includes blue grama and buffalograss.
sources.limits: Modern regional analogue, not a survey identifying this exact graveyard soil or vegetation in 1880.

sources.title: University of Nebraska–Lincoln, Buffalo Grass
sources.supports: Native central/western US short grass with fine blue-green leaves, generally 4–8 inches high.
sources.limits: Modern botanical reference only; no lawn cultivars, mowing pattern or modern landscaping copied.

sources.title: Carol M. Highsmith, Ogallala Boot Hill marker, 2021, LOC highsm.69813
sources.supports: Modern close-up inspected for wood grain and prairie surface context.
sources.limits: Not accepted as evidence of original 1880 marker shape, lettering, age, layout or winter-to-summer colour. No identity or inscription copied.

actual_images_inspected: Both rendered pages of the 2016 walking guide
observations: Guide distinguishes original cemetery from later memorial landscaping.
Plank and rough-cross marker vocabulary supported by text; exact modern pointed/arched marker shapes not treated as original.
Present photo is winter and contemporary; used only for wood-grain context, not summer colour or original architecture.
